summary: The C preprocessor is a text-processing pass that runs before the compiler proper. It pastes in header files, replaces macros, and keeps or drops regions of source according to conditions. It matters because every real C project, from embedded firmware to the Linux kernel, depends on include guards, feature flags and macro helpers, and because careless macros are a classic source of subtle bugs and interview questions.

sections.heading: Overview
sections.body: The preprocessor is the first translation phase you meet. It reads your `.c` file, obeys every line that starts with `#`, and hands a cleaned-up stream of tokens to the compiler. It knows nothing about types, scopes or functions. It only understands tokens, lines and a small expression language for conditions. That is why a macro can do things a function cannot (build a string from a name, paste identifiers together, remove code entirely) and also why it can do things a function would never allow (evaluate an argument twice, capture a surrounding variable by accident).
sections.code:
gcc -E main.c -o main.i    # stop after preprocessing, inspect the result
gcc -S main.i              # then compile to assembly
gcc -c main.c              # or do every phase, ending in main.o

sections.heading: Core Concepts
bullets: **Directive**: a line whose first non-blank token is `#`, such as `#include`, `#define`, `#if`. It ends at the newline unless you continue it with a trailing backslash.
**Object-like macro**: `#define NAME replacement`. Every later use of the token `NAME` is replaced by the replacement tokens.
**Function-like macro**: `#define NAME(a, b) replacement`. The `(` must touch the name. The arguments are substituted as token sequences, not as values.
**Macro expansion**: after substitution the result is rescanned, so a macro can expand to another macro. A macro never expands inside itself (this stops infinite recursion).
**Stringification**: `#x` inside a macro body turns the argument into a string literal.
**Token pasting**: `a ## b` glues two tokens into one new token, for example `var` and `1` into `var1`.
**Conditional compilation**: `#if`, `#ifdef`, `#ifndef`, `#elif`, `#else`, `#endif` keep or discard regions of text before the compiler sees them.
**Include guard**: an `#ifndef X / #define X / #endif` wrapper that makes a header safe to include many times.
**Predefined macros**: names such as `__FILE__`, `__LINE__`, `__DATE__`, `__TIME__`, `__STDC_VERSION__` that the implementation supplies.
**Translation unit**: the output of preprocessing one source file, with every header pasted in. This is what the compiler really compiles.

sections.heading: How It Works
sections.body: The standard describes eight translation phases. Four of them matter for macros. First, trigraphs and line splices (backslash-newline) are handled. Next the text is split into preprocessing tokens and comments become a single space. Then directives run and macros expand. Finally adjacent string literals are concatenated, and only then does real compilation begin. The order explains several oddities: a backslash at the end of a `//` comment continues the comment onto the next line, and comments vanish before `#define` bodies are recorded.

Walk through `SQUARE(LIMIT + 1)`. The preprocessor sees the function-like macro and collects the argument tokens `LIMIT + 1`. It fully expands the argument first (so `LIMIT` becomes `5`), substitutes it for each `x` in the body, and rescans the result. With the parentheses in the body you get `((5 + 1) * (5 + 1))`, which is 36. Without them you would get `5 + 1 * 5 + 1`, which is 11. Compile with `-DDEBUG` and `TRACE` prints file, line and message. Without it `TRACE` becomes `((void)0)`, a no-op that still behaves like an expression statement.

sections.heading: Variants & Types
bullets: **Object-like constant** (`#define N 100`): no type, no scope, no address. Prefer `enum { N = 100 };` for integers or `static const int N = 100;` when you want a real object. Keep `#define` for values needed by `#if` or by array sizes in old compilers.

**Chain macros**: one macro whose body names another (`#define INSTA FOLLOWERS`, `#define FOLLOWERS 138`). Expansion is lazy, so the inner name is looked up at the point of use, not at the point of definition.
**Multi-line macros**: end each line with a backslash. The last line has none. Nothing may follow the backslash, not even a space.
**Function-like macro**: fast to write, no call overhead, works for any type. Pays with double evaluation and no type checking.
**Variadic macro**: `#define LOG(fmt, ...) fprintf(stderr, fmt, __VA_ARGS__)` since C99. `__VA_OPT__` is standard only from C23, GNU offers `##__VA_ARGS__` before that.
**`static inline` function**: typed, evaluated once per argument, debuggable, usually as fast. Pick it whenever a function can express the idea.
**`_Generic` selection** (C11): choose an expression by argument type, often wrapped in a macro to fake overloading.
**X-macros**: define a list once as `X(name, value)` entries and expand it several times with different definitions of `X` to generate enums, name tables and switch cases in sync.

sections.heading: Complexity & Costs
bullets: Preprocessing is linear in the size of the translation unit after includes. A header pulled into 500 source files is parsed 500 times, so include hygiene directly affects build time.

A function-like macro has no call cost, but each use duplicates its body. Ten uses of a 30-token macro add roughly 300 tokens of code for the compiler to parse and possibly for the optimizer to merge.
`#include <stdio.h>` typically expands to a few hundred lines on glibc. A C++ standard header can expand to tens of thousands of lines. Precompiled headers and forward declarations exist to cut this.
A macro argument that has side effects runs once per appearance in the body. `MAX(f(), g())` with a naive `MAX` calls the winner twice, doubling its cost and its side effects.
Macro names live in a single global namespace for the rest of the translation unit. There is no scope, so a name like `max` or `min` can silently rewrite unrelated identifiers in later headers.

sections.heading: Common Pitfalls & Gotchas
bullets: **Missing parentheses around parameters**: `#define SQR(x) x*x` turns `SQR(a+b)` into `a+b*a+b`. Parenthesize every parameter use and the whole body.
**Missing parentheses around the body**: `#define TWICE(x) (x)+(x)` breaks `3 * TWICE(2)` into `3 * (2)+(2)`, giving 8 instead of 12.
**Double evaluation**: `SQR(i++)` expands to `((i++) * (i++))`, which modifies `i` twice without a sequence point. That is undefined behavior, not merely a wrong answer.

**Semicolon after a macro statement**: `#define SWAP(a,b) { int t=a; a=b; b=t; }` fails inside `if (c) SWAP(x,y); else ...` because the stray `;` ends the `if`. Wrap the body in `do { ... } while (0)`.
**Space before the parenthesis**: `#define F (x) x+1` defines an object-like macro whose body starts with `(x)`. For function-like macros write `F(x)` with no gap.
**Hidden variable capture**: a temporary named `t` inside a macro shadows a caller variable called `t`. Use unusual names or avoid temporaries.
**Trailing backslash with a space** after it splits the macro and produces confusing errors.
**Using `#define` for types**: `#define PINT int*` followed by `PINT a, b;` declares only `a` as a pointer. Use `typedef int *pint;`.
**Stringifying an unexpanded macro**: `STR(LIMIT)` gives `"LIMIT"`, not `"5"`. You need two levels, `XSTR(x) STR(x)`, so the argument expands before `#` applies.
**Redefinition**: defining the same name twice with different bodies is a constraint violation. Identical redefinition is allowed. Use `#undef` first when you truly need to change it.

sections.heading: Real-World Use
bullets: **Include guards and `#pragma once`** in every header of every C library.
**Portability layers**: `#if defined(_WIN32)` versus `#elif defined(__linux__)` selects the right system calls and types.
**Feature flags and builds**: `-DNDEBUG` turns `assert` into nothing. `-DDEBUG` enables tracing. Autoconf and CMake feed `config.h` full of `HAVE_*` macros.
**Linux kernel**: `container_of`, `offsetof`, `ARRAY_SIZE`, `BUILD_BUG_ON`, `likely`/`unlikely` and the whole `CONFIG_*` system are macros.
**Logging**: `LOG(level, ...)` macros capture `__FILE__` and `__LINE__` at the call site, which no ordinary function can do.
**Code generation with X-macros**: opcode tables, error-code string tables and register maps stay consistent because they come from one list.
**Compile-time checks**: `static_assert` (C11) and older negative-array-size tricks catch size and layout mistakes before the program runs.

sections.heading: Interview Notes
bullets: **What does the preprocessor do?** It runs before compilation, does textual substitution, file inclusion and conditional selection, and knows nothing about types.
**Macro versus function?** Macro: no call overhead, type-agnostic, can use `#`/`##` and `__LINE__`, but double evaluation and no type safety. Function: typed, single evaluation, debuggable.
**`<file>` versus `"file"`?** Angle brackets search the system include path. Quotes search the including file's directory first and then fall back to the system path.
**Why `do { } while (0)`?** It makes a multi-statement macro behave as one statement, safe in `if`/`else` without braces.
**What is `#` and `##`?** Stringify an argument, and paste two tokens into one.
**Can `#define` be debugged?** Not directly. Use `gcc -E` or `-save-temps` to see the expansion, and `gcc -dM -E - < /dev/null` to list predefined macros.

subtopics.title: Stringification and token pasting
subtopics.summary: `#x` makes a string, `a ## b` makes a new identifier, and both need a second level to expand arguments first.

sections.heading: Operators
sections.body: Inside a function-like macro body, `#param` replaces the argument with a string literal containing its spelling (with whitespace normalized and quotes and backslashes escaped). `left ## right` removes the whitespace around the operator and joins the two tokens, and the result must be a valid token. Neither operator expands its operands first, which is the source of the classic two-level trick.
sections.code:
#define STR(x)  #x
#define XSTR(x) STR(x)
#define CAT(a, b)  a##b
#define XCAT(a, b) CAT(a, b)
#define VERSION 3

printf("%s\n", STR(VERSION));    /* VERSION */
printf("%s\n", XSTR(VERSION));   /* 3 */
int CAT(count, 1) = 0;           /* int count1 = 0; */
int XCAT(v, VERSION) = 0;        /* int v3 = 0; */

sections.heading: Typical uses
sections.body: Print the name of an expression in a test macro (`#define CHECK(e) if(!(e)) puts("failed: " #e)`), build function names such as `handler_##name`, and generate families of similar structs or accessors. Adjacent string literals concatenate, so `"failed: " #e` works without any helper function.

subtopics.title: Predefined macros
subtopics.summary: The compiler supplies location and environment macros you can use for logging and portability.

bullets: `__FILE__`: the source file name as a string literal.
`__LINE__`: the current line number as an integer constant.
`__func__` (C99): not a macro but a predefined identifier holding the current function name. `__FUNCTION__` is a GNU spelling.
`__DATE__` and `__TIME__`: build date as `"Mmm dd yyyy"` and time as `"hh:mm:ss"`. They make builds non-reproducible, so many projects avoid them.
`__STDC__`: 1 on conforming implementations. `__STDC_VERSION__`: `199901L` for C99, `201112L` for C11, `201710L` for C17.
`__COUNTER__` (GCC, Clang, MSVC): an integer that increments on every use, handy for unique names.
`__cplusplus`: defined only when compiled as C++, used in headers to add `extern "C"`.

sections.body: List every macro your compiler predefines with `gcc -dM -E - < /dev/null`. You will see `__x86_64__`, `__linux__`, `__GNUC__`, `__SIZEOF_INT__` and hundreds more. These are the right way to branch on architecture, OS and word size.

subtopics.title: Safe multi-statement macros
subtopics.summary: Use `do { ... } while (0)` and unique names so a macro acts like one statement.

sections.body: A macro that expands to several statements breaks when used as the body of an unbraced `if`. Wrapping in a bare block fixes that case but fails when the caller writes a semicolon before `else`. The `do { ... } while (0)` form consumes exactly one trailing semicolon, runs once, and keeps temporaries in their own scope.

With GCC or Clang you can use statement expressions and `typeof` to also avoid double evaluation, for example `({ typeof(a) _a = (a); typeof(b) _b = (b); _a > _b ? _a : _b; })`. These are extensions, not standard C, so a portable library should prefer a `static inline` function when the type is fixed.

subtopics.title: Macros versus inline functions
subtopics.summary: A `static inline` function usually matches macro speed and avoids all the textual traps.

sections.body: Compilers inline small functions on their own at `-O1` and above, so the old performance argument for macros is weak. A function checks argument types, evaluates each argument once, appears in a debugger and in stack traces, and respects scope. Reach for a macro only when you need something a function cannot do.
bullets: **Use a macro for**: stringification, token pasting, `__FILE__`/`__LINE__` capture, conditional compilation, constants needed by the preprocessor, and type-generic helpers when `_Generic` is too clumsy.
**Use a function for**: everything else, especially anything with side-effecting arguments or more than two lines of logic.
**Constants**: `enum` and `static const` respect scope and appear in the debugger. `#define` constants do not.

subtopics.title: Conditional compilation and include guards
subtopics.summary: Select code per platform or build, and make headers idempotent.

sections.body: `#if` evaluates an integer constant expression. Undefined identifiers count as 0, and `defined(NAME)` (or `defined NAME`) tests existence. `#elif` chains alternatives. `#ifdef X` is shorthand for `#if defined(X)`. Conditions cannot use `sizeof`, casts or enum constants, because the preprocessor does not know about types.

sections.heading: Include guards
sections.body: A header included twice through different paths would redeclare its types, which is an error for `struct` definitions. The guard macro name should be unique, usually derived from the path, for example `PROJECT_NET_SOCKET_H`. `#pragma once` is shorter and accepted by every mainstream compiler, though it is not in the standard.
sections.code:
#ifndef PROJECT_VECTOR_H
#define PROJECT_VECTOR_H
typedef struct { int *data; size_t len, cap; } Vector;
#endif /* PROJECT_VECTOR_H */

subtopics.title: Other directives: #undef, #error, #line, #pragma
subtopics.summary: Smaller directives that control macro lifetime, diagnostics and compiler hints.

bullets: **`#undef NAME`**: removes a macro so you can redefine it or stop it leaking into later code. Undefining a name that is not defined is allowed.
**`#error message`**: stops compilation with your message. Pair with `#if` to reject unsupported configurations. `#warning` is a common extension.
**`#line N "file"`**: overrides `__LINE__` and `__FILE__`, used by generators such as lex and yacc so errors point at the original source.
**`#pragma`**: implementation-defined hints, for example `#pragma pack(push, 1)` for struct packing, `#pragma once`, and `#pragma GCC diagnostic`. Unknown pragmas are ignored.
**`_Pragma("...")`**: the operator form of `#pragma`, usable inside macro bodies.
**Null directive**: a lone `#` on a line does nothing.

subtopics.title: Inspecting expansion and debugging macros
subtopics.summary: Use the compiler to show what a macro really became.

sections.body: When a macro misbehaves, look at its expansion. `gcc -E file.c | less` prints the translation unit after preprocessing, with `# 12 "file.c"` line markers. `-P` suppresses those markers. `-C` keeps comments. `-dD` leaves the `#define` lines in the output so you can see definitions in order. For a single macro, write a tiny file that uses it and run `-E` on that. Remember that error messages from inside a macro point at the use site, and GCC adds a note such as "in expansion of macro 'X'" to help you trace it.

subtopics.title: X-macros and generated tables
subtopics.summary: Write a list once, expand it several times to keep enums and strings in sync.

sections.body: An X-macro is a list macro whose entries call an undefined helper `X`. Before each use you define `X` to produce what you need, then undefine it. Adding a new entry then updates every derived table automatically, which removes a whole class of out-of-sync bugs between an enum and its name array.

takeaways: The preprocessor is pure text and token substitution: it runs before compilation and knows nothing about types or scopes.
Parenthesize every macro parameter and the whole body, or precedence will bite: `SQR(a+b)` must not become `a+b*a+b`.
Arguments with side effects (`i++`) are evaluated once per appearance in the macro body, which can be undefined behavior.
Use `do { ... } while (0)` for multi-statement macros and a `static inline` function whenever a function is enough.
`#x` stringifies and `a ## b` pastes, and you need a two-level wrapper (`XSTR`) to expand a macro argument first.
Guard every header with `#ifndef`/`#define`/`#endif` or `#pragma once`.
`gcc -E` shows exactly what the compiler will see and is the first tool to reach for when a macro misbehaves.

practice.title: Predict the output of `SQR(2+3)` for `#define SQR(x) x*x` and fix the macro
Write include guards for a header and say why the guard name must be unique
Write a MAX macro that evaluates each argument only once using GCC extensions, then without them
Why does `SWAP(a,b)` as a braced block fail before an `else`, and how does do-while(0) fix it?
Make `PRINT_VAR(x)` print the variable name and its value using `#`
Use X-macros to generate an enum and a matching string table
Implement a LOG macro that adds file and line and compiles to nothing in release builds
Explain why `STR(VERSION)` prints VERSION and write `XSTR` so it prints the number
Count the bugs in `#define ABS(x) x<0?-x:x` and write a correct version
